chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ali ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) said:
I asked my brother Musa (peace be upon him): Does the person in ihram wear the garment dyed with safflower? He said: 'If there is no perfume in it, there is no harm with it.'

key_terms.الْعُصْفُرِ: safflower (a plant used for yellow dye)
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: the person in the state of ihram
key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm with it (it is permissible)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a pilgrim in ihram to wear clothes dyed with safflower?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS) clarifies a specific nuance in the prohibition of scented garments for the muhrim, distinguishing between the dye itself and any added perfume. In Shia fiqh, this highlights the principle that the impurity lies in the scent (tayyib) rather than the color or material, allowing for garments dyed with safflower provided no fragrance is present. This ruling is often discussed alongside the broader prohibition of covering the head and wearing stitched clothes, emphasizing the simplicity of the ihram state.
